# 0 · Getting set up and what you are looking at [12 min]{.timing}

**R** is a programming language for working with data. **Positron** is the
program we use to *talk to* R — an integrated development environment (IDE).
R does the work; Positron is the workshop it happens in.

## Setup checklist (do once, before class if you can)

> Need bigger, step-by-step instructions? See [**Prep — Getting Set Up**](../../week_0/prep/setup_positron.qmd).

::: {.callout-note title="Prep page"}
- Big-font, step-by-step version for the projector: [**Prep — Getting Set Up**](../../week_0/prep/setup_positron.qmd) (also covers the Session tab and LM/YT)
:::

Check each box as you finish it:

- [ ] **1. Install R, then Positron.** Download R from
  <https://cloud.r-project.org> and install it. Then download Positron from
  <https://positron.posit.co> and install it. (R first — Positron needs to
  find it.)
- [ ] **2. Download today's file.** From the course site, download the
  `.qmd` file for today. The file name has today's date and `qmd 1` in
  it — that is this document.
- [ ] **3. Build your folders on the Desktop.** On your Desktop, create:
  - a folder named `R`
  - a folder named `Data`
  - inside `R`, two folders: `Notes` and `Labs`

  When you are done it looks like this:

  ```
  Desktop/
  ├── R/
  │   ├── Notes/
  │   └── Labs/
  └── Data/
  ```
- [ ] **4. Move the file.** Drag the downloaded `.qmd` file out of
  `Downloads` and into `Desktop/R/Notes/`. (Notes go in `Notes`; labs will
  go in `Labs`; data files will go in `Data`. Every week.)
- [ ] **5. Open Positron.**
- [ ] **6. Open your folder.** In Positron: **File → Open Folder…** and
  choose `Desktop/R`. The folder's contents appear in the left sidebar.
- [ ] **7. Open the file.** In the left sidebar, click `Notes`, then click
  the `.qmd` file. It opens in the middle of the screen — you are now
  reading it inside Positron.
- [ ] **8. Fill in your name and date** at the top of this document.

::: {.callout-important title="Teaching note — setup"}
- The eight setup steps should be done **before** class: install R → install Positron → download the `.qmd` → make `Desktop/R/{Notes,Labs}` and `Desktop/Data` → move the file into `R/Notes` → open Positron → **File → Open Folder…** on `Desktop/R` → open the file from the sidebar → fill in name and date
- Budget **3 minutes** at the start to rescue whoever isn't there yet
- Most common failures:
  - the file is still in `Downloads`
  - they opened the *file* rather than the *folder*, so the Explorer sidebar is empty
- Fix for both: **File → Open Folder… → `Desktop/R`**
- Make them fill in name and date — first thing they type into a `.qmd`, and how you tell whose render is whose
:::

## The panes [6 min]{.timing}

Positron is divided into **panes**. The numbers in the picture match the
list below — find each one on *your* screen and check it off. Physically
point at it.

![Positron's panes. Your screen will look like this, with your `.qmd` open in the Editor instead of the Welcome page.](images/positron_panes.png){width=100%}

- [ ] **1 · Editor** — the big middle area where this `.qmd` file is open.
  Code you *keep* lives here.
- [ ] **2 · Console** — bottom of the screen, the tab labeled **CONSOLE**.
  R answers here, one command at a time. Code you type here is *not saved*.
- [ ] **3 · Variables** — right side, under the **SESSION** tab. Every object
  you create this session shows up here. (Right now it says *No variables
  have been created* — remember what that looks like.)
- [ ] **4 · Plots** — right side, below Variables. Pictures appear here.
- [ ] **5 · Explorer** — the top icon in the left sidebar (two overlapping
  pages). Click it to see the files in the folder you opened.
- [ ] **6 · Session** — the `R 4.x.x` label in the top-right corner. More on
  this in a moment.
- [ ] **7 · Terminal** — the tab next to Console at the bottom. It is *not*
  R; it talks to your computer's operating system. Know it exists; we will
  not use it today.
- [ ] **Help** — opens on the right side when you ask R for documentation
  (section 3 today).

::: {.callout-important title="Teaching note — panes"}
- Put the annotated screenshot (`images/positron_panes.png`) on the projector
- Have students physically point at each numbered pane — the checklist **is** the activity
- Use Positron's own names consistently: **Editor**, **Console**, **Variables**, **Plots**, **Explorer**
- Two traps:
  - **CONSOLE** and **TERMINAL** tabs sit side by side — the Terminal shows a `%` prompt, not `>`
  - Variables/Plots live inside the **SESSION** panel on the right — if closed, the right side looks blank
- Terminal / Viewer / Connections get one sentence each — resist the tour becoming the lesson
:::

> *YT1 (1 min). A neighbor asks "where do I look to see what objects I've
> made?" Which pane do you point at? **Variables***
>
> *YT2 (1 min). You type code and want it to be there tomorrow. Which pane
> does it go in? **The Editor (this `.qmd`)***

::: {.callout-tip title="Answers"}
- [YT1]{.yt} Variables
- [YT2]{.yt} the Editor (this `.qmd`)
:::

## The Session [6 min]{.timing}

R runs inside a **session** — a running copy of R that Positron is talking to.

**How to get to the Session tab.** Look at the **top-right corner** of
Positron (arrow **6** in the picture). It shows which R is running, something
like `R 4.5.1`. That label *is* your session. Click it once: a small menu
opens showing the running R, a **Restart** button, a **Shutdown** button, and
any other interpreters installed on your computer. Close the menu (press
Escape). Now look just below it on the right side: the panel labeled
**SESSION** holds the **Variables** and **Plots** panes — everything the
session is holding in memory, made visible.

Three things to know about the session, today:

1. **It has memory.** Every object you create lives in the session, and shows
   up in Variables.
2. **It can be restarted.** The Restart button (top-right session menu, or the
   Console toolbar) wipes the session's memory clean — Variables empties out.
   Your *files* are untouched.
3. **It can be replaced.** The same menu lets you pick a different R (or
   Python) if more than one is installed. Don't do that today; just know the
   button exists.

Do this now: create nothing yet, look at Variables (empty), and remember what
empty looks like — we'll come back after we've made some objects.

::: {.callout-important title="Teaching note — getting to the Session tab"}
- Point at the top-right interpreter label (`R 4.x.x`, arrow 6 on the screenshot)
- Click it once so they see the menu: running session, Restart, Shutdown, other interpreters — then press Escape
- Point at the **SESSION** panel beneath it: *"that label is the session; this panel is what the session remembers"*
- Say the three facts — **memory / restartable / replaceable** — and move on
- Payoff comes in §4 LM11 when they restart for real
- Show that Variables is empty *now* — the "before" picture makes the restart in §4 land
:::

> *Q1. In one sentence: what is the difference between the Console and the
> Editor?*
>
> *Your answer: The Console runs code once and forgets it; the Editor holds
> code you keep, so you can re-run everything tomorrow.*

::: {.callout-tip title="Q1 model answer"}
- [Q1]{.q} The Console runs code once and forgets it
- The Editor holds code you keep, so you can re-run everything tomorrow
:::

# 1 · Running code and code chunks [12 min]{.timing}

**LM1 — the Console (2 min).** Click into the Console, type `2 + 2`, press
Enter. R answers. Now press the up-arrow — the Console remembers your last
line. Edit it to `2 + 3` and press Enter.

**LM2 — a code chunk (5 min).** This document is a **Quarto** file: text and
code mixed together. The gray boxes are **code chunks**. A chunk is:

- opened by a line that reads ```` ```{r} ```` (three backticks, then `{r}`)
- closed by a line of three backticks ```` ``` ````
- everything between the two is R code

Look at the chunk below in the Editor. Notice the small **play button** at
its top-right corner. Click it (or put your cursor on a line and press
**Cmd/Ctrl + Enter** to run just that line):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LM2: this line is a COMMENT — R ignores anything after #
2 + 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
3 * 7
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 21
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
10 / 4
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 2.5
```


:::
:::


Two things happened: the results appeared **under the chunk** *and* the same
code ran in the **Console**. A chunk is just a saved bundle of Console lines.

**LM3 — chunk options (2 min).** Lines that start with `#|` at the top of a
chunk are **options** — instructions to Quarto, not R. You will see
`#| eval: false` in this document; it means "show this code, but don't run
it when rendering." Useful for code that is broken on purpose.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LM3: this chunk is displayed but never runs
this_would_be_an_error
```
:::


::: {.callout-important title="Teaching notes — LM1–LM3"}
- [LM1]{.lm} The up-arrow trick saves students dozens of retypes this term — worth the 20 seconds
- [LM2]{.lm} **Anatomy of a chunk:**
  - put the cursor on the ```` ```{r} ```` line and name its parts out loud: fence, `{r}` = "this is R", fence
  - click the play button so they see output land **both** under the chunk and in the Console
  - the sentence to leave them with: *"a chunk is a saved bundle of Console lines"*
  - students create their own chunks starting Monday (Foundations 02) — today they only run and edit ours
- [LM3]{.lm} One sentence on `#|` options is enough — they'll write `#| label:` and `#| eval: false` themselves in ETV cycles
:::

> *YT3 (3 min). Edit the chunk below so it computes THREE things: 5 minus
> something to give 1; 100 divided by 8; and 2 to the 10th power (hint: `^`).*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# YT3: edit and run — start with:  5 - ____
5 - 4
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
100 / 8
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 12.5
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
2^10
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 1024
```


:::
:::


> *Q2. Where did the output show up — under the chunk, in the Console, or
> both? **Both***

::: {.callout-note title="Expected — YT3"}
- [YT3]{.yt} `1` · `12.5` · `1024`
- [Q2]{.q} **both** (output appears under the chunk *and* in the Console)

# 2 · Objects and assignment [16 min]{.timing}

**LM4 — the arrow (3 min).** `<-` stores a value under a name. Without it,
R computes and forgets. (Type it fast: `Alt + -` inserts `<-` in Positron.)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LM4: create an object, then call its name
cups <- 3
cups
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 3
```


:::
:::


Look at the **Variables pane** — `cups` is there now, with its value.

**LM5 — objects combine (4 min).** Predict before you run: what will `total`
be?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LM5: predict, then run
price <- 4.50
total <- cups * price
total
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 13.5
```


:::
:::


> *Q3. Prediction: **13.5**  · What R said: **13.5***

**LM6 — overwriting (4 min).** Run this, then check the Variables pane again.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LM6: same name, new value
cups <- 10
total
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 13.5
```


:::
:::


> *Q4. `total` did NOT change to 45. Why not? (Hint: WHEN was `total`
> computed?)*
>
> *Your answer: `total` was computed at the moment the `<-` line ran, using
> `cups = 3`. Changing `cups` later doesn't re-run old lines — R objects store
> values, not formulas.*

::: {.callout-tip title="Q4 model answer — the most important idea of the day"}
- [Q4]{.q} `total` was computed *at the moment* the `<-` line ran, using `cups = 3`
- Changing `cups` later doesn't re-run old lines — **R objects store values, not formulas**
- Spend the full minutes here
- Spreadsheet contrast lands well: Excel cells recompute; R objects don't
:::

> *YT4 (5 min). In the chunk below:*
> *(a) create `hours` holding how many hours you slept last night;*
> *(b) create `minutes` as `hours` times 60;*
> *(c) print `minutes`;*
> *(d) predict — if you now change `hours` to 8, does `minutes` change? Test it.*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# YT4: any sleep value; e.g.
hours   <- 7
minutes <- hours * 60
minutes
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 420
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
hours   <- 8
minutes            # still 420 — same lesson as Q4, now self-discovered
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 420
```


:::
:::


> *Your prediction for (d): **No — `minutes` stays 420** · What happened: **It stayed 420***

::: {.callout-tip title="YT4 (d) answer"}
- [YT4]{.yt} `minutes` does **not** change — Q4 again, but the student built it, so it sticks
- Have two students say their prediction and result aloud
- Then point at Variables: `cups`, `price`, `total`, `hours`, `minutes` — five objects, all session memory
:::

Now look at Variables: how many objects are there? Names are on the left,
values on the right — this pane is your session's memory, made visible.

The `$` pulls one column out of it (much more on `$` next week).


::: {.cell}

```

```

:::

- [LM7]{.lm} `20.09062` · `32`

**LM8 — help (5 min).** Every function has documentation. Run this, and the
Help pane opens:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
?mean
```
:::


Read the **Usage** and **Arguments** sections. That's where the answers to
"what does this function want from me?" always live.

> *Q5. From the help page: what does the `na.rm` argument do?*
>
> *Your answer: `na.rm = TRUE` tells `mean()` to remove `NA` values before
> computing; the default `FALSE` returns `NA` if any value is missing.*

> *YT6 (2 min). Look up `?round`. What is the name of its second argument,
> and what is its default value? **`digits`** · **`0`***

**LM9 — packages (5 min).** A **package** is a collection of functions
someone wrote. You **install** once (download to your computer), you **load**
every session (open the toolbox):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("tidyverse")   # ONCE per computer — done in setup
library(tidyverse)              # EVERY session you use it
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LM9: load it now (already installed)
library(tidyverse)
```
:::


> *Q6. Fill the blanks: install.packages() runs **once** per computer;
> library() runs **once** per session.*

::: {.callout-tip title="Q5 · YT6 · Q6 answers"}
- [Q5]{.q} `na.rm = TRUE` tells `mean()` to remove `NA` values before computing; the default `FALSE` returns `NA` if any value is missing
  - plant the flag: this argument returns in Foundations 03 and every ETV cycle
- [YT6]{.yt} `digits`, default `0` — the purpose is reading a Usage line, not the fact itself
- [Q6]{.q} install runs **once per computer**; library runs **once every session**
  - analogy that sticks: install = buying the drill; library = taking it out of the garage
:::

# 4 · When things break [12 min]{.timing}

**LM10 — read the error (4 min).** Run this broken line. Read the message
*slowly* before fixing it.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LM10: broken on purpose — fix it in the chunk below
meen(mtcars$mpg)
#> Error in meen(mtcars$mpg) : could not find function "meen"
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# LM10 fixed:
mean(mtcars$mpg)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 20.09062
```


:::
:::


> *Q7. What did the error message say, and what did it mean?*
>
> *Your answer: `could not find function "meen"` — the name doesn't exist:
> a typo, or a package not loaded.*

::: {.callout-tip title="Q7 model answer"}
- [Q7]{.q} "could not find function" means the *name* doesn't exist — a typo, or a package not loaded
- Name the two most common error families now:
  - `could not find function` → typo / `library()` missing
  - `object not found` → name typo / never created
- Students who can *classify* an error stop fearing errors
:::

> *YT7 (4 min). Each chunk below has ONE bug. Read the error, then fix it
> in place. Write the error family in the comment (typo in a function name?
> object that doesn't exist? something else?).*


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# YT7a — error family: ____
mean(mtcars$mgp)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# YT7a — error family: column-name typo (`$` on a missing column gives NULL, not an error)
mean(mtcars$mpg)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 20.09062
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# YT7b — error family: ____
mean(Mtcars$mpg)
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# YT7b — error family: object not found (R is case-sensitive)
mean(mtcars$mpg)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 20.09062
```


:::
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# YT7c — error family: ____
mean(mtcars$mpg
```
:::



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# YT7c — error family: unbalanced parentheses (missing `)`)
mean(mtcars$mpg)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 20.09062
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-caution title="YT7 answers — three error families"}
- [YT7a]{.yt} `mtcars$mgp` → returns `NULL`; `mean` warns "argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA"
  - family: **column-name typo** — `$` on a missing column gives `NULL`, not an error (the sneakiest of the three)
  - fix: `mpg`
- [YT7b]{.yt} `Mtcars` → `Error: object 'Mtcars' not found`
  - family: **object not found** — R is case-sensitive
  - fix: `mtcars`
- [YT7c]{.yt} missing `)` → Console shows a `+` prompt waiting for more; in a chunk, "unexpected end of input"
  - family: **unbalanced parentheses**
  - fix: add `)` — and show them **Escape** in the Console to get out of a `+` prompt
:::

**LM11 — the reset button (4 min).** If R gets confused, restart the session:
Console toolbar → **Restart R** (or the top-right session menu). Do it now,
for real. Then look at Variables.

> *Q8. After the restart: is `cups` still in Variables? **No** · Is the code
> that CREATED `cups` still in this file? **Yes** · Re-run section 2's chunks —
> how long did it take to get `cups` back? **About 10 seconds***

::: {.callout-important title="LM11 — restart for real"}
- [LM11]{.lm} Everyone restarts → Variables empties
- [Q8]{.q} `cups` gone · code still here · re-running §2 takes ~10 seconds
- That 10-second recovery *is* the argument for putting code in the file
:::

# 5 · Save & render [8 min]{.timing}

Save this file into your project's `R/` folder as
`fnd01_yourlastname.qmd`, then press **Render** (the button above the
Editor, or Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + K). A webpage appears — your first
reproducible document. Every chunk in it re-ran from a *fresh* session to
build that page.

> *Exit question: name one thing that lives in the Variables pane and one
> thing that lives in the Editor, and say which one survives a restart.*
>
> *Your answer: `cups` lives in Variables and is gone after a restart; this
> `.qmd` (and the code that recreates `cups`) lives in the Editor and
> survives.*

::: {.callout-tip title="Exit model answer"}
- `cups` lives in Variables → gone after restart
- this `.qmd` lives in the Editor → survives
- the code that *recreates* `cups` survives — the entire argument for reproducible documents, made on day one without ever saying "CLO 9"
:::
